answer_text:
We take \(H(0)=0\). Since the integrand is bounded, the improper integral is well-defined near \(0\).

Differentiability at \(0\) requires the limit
\[
H'(0)=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{H(x)-H(0)}{x-0}=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x}\int_0^x \left|\sin\frac1t\right|\,dt.
\]

First consider \(x>0\). Let \(u=1/t\), so \(t=1/u\) and \(dt=-u^{-2}\,du\). Then
\[
\int_0^x \left|\sin\frac1t\right|\,dt
=
\int_{1/x}^{\infty}\frac{|\sin u|}{u^2}\,du.
\]
Set \(y=1/x\). Then
\[
\frac{H(x)}{x}
=
y\int_y^\infty \frac{|\sin u|}{u^2}\,du.
\]

The mean value of \(|\sin u|\) over one period is
\[
m=\frac{2}{\pi}.
\]
Write
\[
|\sin u|=m+h(u),
\]
where \(h\) is periodic with mean zero. Its primitive
\[
P(u)=\int_0^u h(v)\,dv
\]
is bounded, say \(|P(u)|\le M\).

Then
\[
\int_y^\infty \frac{|\sin u|}{u^2}\,du
=
m\int_y^\infty \frac{du}{u^2}
+
\int_y^\infty \frac{h(u)}{u^2}\,du
=
\frac{m}{y}
+
\int_y^\infty \frac{h(u)}{u^2}\,du.
\]
Integrating by parts,
\[
\int_y^\infty \frac{h(u)}{u^2}\,du
=
-\frac{P(y)}{y^2}
+
2\int_y^\infty \frac{P(u)}{u^3}\,du,
\]
so
\[
\left|\int_y^\infty \frac{h(u)}{u^2}\,du\right|
\le
\frac{M}{y^2}+2M\int_y^\infty \frac{du}{u^3}
=
\frac{2M}{y^2}.
\]
Thus
\[
\int_y^\infty \frac{|\sin u|}{u^2}\,du
=
\frac{m}{y}+O\left(\frac1{y^2}\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{H(x)}{x}
=
y\left(\frac{m}{y}+O\left(\frac1{y^2}\right)\right)
=
m+O\left(\frac1y\right)
\to m
\qquad (x\to 0^+).
\]
So the right-hand derivative is
\[
H'_+(0)=\frac{2}{\pi}.
\]

Now note that
\[
\left|\sin\frac1{(-t)}\right|=\left|\sin\frac1t\right|,
\]
so the integrand is even. Hence \(H\) is odd, and
\[
\frac{H(x)}{x}
\]
has the same limit from the left. Therefore
\[
\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{H(x)}{x}=\frac{2}{\pi}.
\]

Thus \(H\) is differentiable at \(x=0\), and
\[
\boxed{\text{Yes, }H\text{ is differentiable at }0\text{ with }H'(0)=\frac{2}{\pi}}
\]
